verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a psalm, David's own.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is not part of the poem but of the performance score, and the KJV numbers it as verse 0 while the Hebrew counts it as verse 1. 'To the choirmaster' (lamnatzeach) names the Temple musician in charge; the root natzach means 'to be preeminent, to excel', which is why the KJV has 'chief Musician'. 'Of David' (ledavid) can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of' David; the Hebrew preposition does not decide. Later tradition tied this psalm to David's flight from Saul, when Doeg and the Ziphites informed on him (Radak, Meiri and Malbim on this verse); the text itself gives no such setting, so treat that as an old reading, not a given.

philological_notes.note: A title for the director of the Temple music, from the root 'to excel, to lead'. It stands over many psalms and tells the performers that this one belongs to the liturgical collection.
A song sung to an instrument; the root zamar means 'to make music', specifically plucked or struck strings. It is the standard label of a Psalter song.

verses.translation_literal: Rescue me, YHWH, from an evil man; from a man of violent acts you will keep me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pull me out, LORD. Out of the grip of an evil man, out of the reach of a man whose hands are all violence. Guard me.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens with an imperative, no greeting, no praise. The speaker is cornered, so he starts on the verb. 'Rescue' (chaletzeni) is the word for drawing something out, as one slips off a sandal (Deut 25:9) or draws a sword. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'taking out and pulling out'. Picture someone hauled out of a pit or off a hook. The KJV's 'Deliver me' is accurate but pale. The second line shifts to an imperfect 'you will keep me' (tintzereni), which the Hebrew can read as a wish or as a confident statement; the KJV chooses the wish ('preserve me') and the YLT the statement ('thou keepest me'). A good performance can hold both. 'Man of violence' (ish chamasim) uses the plural, 'violent acts': the man is made of them. Chamas is the word that the flood story gives as the reason for the flood (Gen 6:11), not just brawling but ruthless injustice. The KJV 'evil man' is fair, although the Hebrew sets 'adam' (a human being, someone frail) beside the harder 'ish', so the evil is committed by mere humans, which makes the appeal to YHWH the more urgent.

philological_notes.note: Imperative: 'pull me out, draw me out'. The root is used for taking off a sandal, drawing off a shoe, and for taking a soldier out of the ranks. Meiri compares the removal of a shoe (Deut 25:9) and the stones taken out of a leprous house (Lev 14:40).
A plural abstract, 'acts of violence': the one who deals in them. The Meiri notes that 'a man of violence' names any wicked person who wrongs the good in any way, even without theft.

verses.translation_literal: Who have planned evils in the heart; every day they stir up wars.
verses.translation_dramatic: They are the ones who turn evil over in their hearts, and day after day they stir up quarrels until they become wars.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'heart' in Hebrew is the place of thinking, not of feeling, so 'planned evils in the heart' means they are scheming with the mind (chashav, the root of 'to calculate'). The plural 'evils' (ra'ot) stays plural: a heap of separate bad plans. The second line has a famous crux. The verb yaguru is either from gur I 'to gather' (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David: 'they gather wars' as one collects things; Radak and Metzudat Zion compare 'he gathers it in his net', Hab 1:15) or from gur II 'to stir up strife', as in 'do not stir yourself against them' (Deut 2:5, Ibn Ezra's second root). The KJV takes the first ('gathered together for war'), which turns the abstract plural 'wars' into an army and has them assemble; the ASV does the same. The Hebrew says they gather or stir up wars, a mental activity: the quarrels are what they collect. Rashi reads it differently again: wars happen in their dwellings (megurehem). Keep the ambiguity in your delivery as a continuous, restless menace.

philological_notes.note: Either 'they gather' (gur I, as in Hab 1:15, Radak and Metzudat Zion) or 'they stir up (strife)' (gur II). Rashi hears 'dwell' (megurim), so wars are in their dwellings. No form decides; the line works with either.

verses.translation_literal: They have sharpened their tongue like a snake; venom of a viper is under their lips. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: They hone their tongues to a point, like a snake's. Under their lips lies the venom of a viper. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the psalm's most famous image, and Paul quotes the second half in Romans 3:13. The verb shananu belongs to blades and arrows: you whet a sword, you sharpen an arrow (Ps 45:6). The tongue is made into a weapon with the same verb. The snake's flickering tongue was the ancient impression of a sting, which Radak and Meiri use to explain the comparison: the snake gathers and points its tongue before it bites. Two animal words are doubled: nachash is the ordinary snake, and 'akhshuv (a hapax, found only here) is a viper or some other biting thing, and Rashi, with the Targum, takes it as a spider. The KJV's 'adders' poison' picks the snake. The Hebrew chemat is 'venom', not 'heat'; Rashi proves it by Deut 32:33, where wine is called the 'chemat of serpents', and a heat of rage would not sit beside wine. KJV 'under their lips' is exact: poison is kept in the mouth sac behind the lips. Selah closes the first movement; its meaning is lost, and Ibn Ezra, reading it as 'truly', makes it an amen on the accusation.

philological_notes.note: Occurs only here. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as a kind of poisonous snake, 'one of the species of the serpent, hard and very evil'. Rashi and the Targum read 'spider'. I follow the snake reading but flag the dispute.
'Venom', as in Deut 32:33 and 32:24 (cited by Rashi and Metzudat Zion), not 'heat' or 'wrath'. The same noun can mean either; the context of the mouth makes it poison.

verses.translation_literal: Keep me, YHWH, from the hands of a wicked man; from a man of violent acts you will keep me, who have planned to push my steps.
verses.translation_dramatic: Guard me, LORD, from the hands of the wicked. Keep me from the man who deals in violence, from those who have schemed to knock the ground out from under my steps.
verses.directors_commentary: The petition returns, this time with two different verbs for 'keep': shamar (guard, as a watchman does) and natzar (preserve, protect, as one guards a vineyard or a secret). The line repeats verse 2 ('from a man of violent acts') almost word for word, which makes the psalm a circular prayer: he comes back to the same fear again and again. 'From the hands of' is idiom for power and reach, not for literal hands. The last clause goes beyond the KJV's 'overthrow my goings'. The verb lidchot means 'to push, to thrust down', as a wall is pushed over or a person shoved off his footing (Ps 118:13, 'you pushed me hard that I might fall', cited by Meiri), and pe'amai, 'my steps', is literally 'my footfalls' (Metzudat Zion compares Isa 26:6). So they plan to trip him, not to overthrow a government. 'Goings' in the KJV is archaic for 'steps'. Note the shift of tense: the 'who have planned' has a perfect verb, so the plot is already laid.

philological_notes.note: 'To push, thrust down, make fall'. Used of shoving someone off their footing. Ibn Ezra compares 'my feet from stumbling' (Ps 56:14 and 116:8), Meiri 'you pushed me hard that I might fall' (Ps 118:13).
'My steps', literally 'my footfalls' or 'my beats' (the same noun means a time or occasion). Metzudat Zion glosses it 'my feet, from the stepping with them', citing Isa 26:6.

verses.translation_literal: The proud have hidden a trap for me, and cords; they have spread a net at the side of a track; snares they have set for me. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The proud have buried a trap for me, and cords with it. They have spread a net beside the path I walk. They have laid snares for me. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker now turns from the people to the equipment. He lists four hunting devices in a row: a pit-trap (pach), cords (chavalim), a net (reshet) and snares (moqeshim). It is a bird-catcher's and a game-hunter's kit, and the enemies are the hunters. Rashi describes the net with a long rope tied to its edge, which the fowler pulls when the birds settle beneath it. The KJV's 'gins' is an archaic word for 'traps' (from 'engine') and its 'wayside' is accurate but vague, since ma'gal is a rutted cart-track, the path he regularly takes. That is the point: they have studied his habits and set the traps on the route he walks every day. 'The proud' (ge'im) has a sharper edge in Hebrew than in English; it is the swaggering, the self-exalted, and prepares the line 'they exalt themselves' in verse 9. Notice the repeated 'for me' (li) at the beginning and the end: the trap is made to the speaker's measure. Selah ends the second movement.

philological_notes.note: A track worn by wheels or feet, from the root of 'wheel, circle'. Metzudat Zion compares 'he leads me in tracks of righteousness' (Ps 23:3). Rashi: the track of his steps, which the hunters have watched.
Snares; the word gives the thing that catches by springing. It is often used metaphorically for the temptations or plots that bring a person down.

verses.translation_literal: I said to YHWH, "My God are you." Give ear, YHWH, to the sound of my supplications.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I said to the LORD, "You are my God." Listen, LORD. Listen to the sound of my pleading.
verses.directors_commentary: The pace changes. After five verses of 'they', the speaker says 'I', the first time. 'I said to YHWH' reports a decision, spoken aloud: not 'I thought', but 'I said'. The confession 'My God are you' puts the pronoun after the predicate, which in Hebrew gives it weight: Mine, you are my God. This is the oldest covenant language, but spoken here as a refusal to rely on himself (Ibn Ezra on this verse: 'I have no power to escape them, only you'). The KJV 'hear the voice of my supplications' is literal enough, but the Hebrew verb ha'azinah is from the noun 'ear': 'give ear', 'turn your ear toward'. Taking 'ozen' (ear) as a verb is a vivid image: bend down your ear. The plural 'supplications' (tachanunai) comes from the root for 'grace' (chen), so these are pleas for favour, not demands for justice. A director should make the actor lower the voice here: it is the quietest line of the opening movement.

philological_notes.note: A denominative verb from 'ozen', ear: 'give ear, incline your ear'. With the added -ah ending it is a polite, urgent imperative.
Plural, 'pleas for favour', from the root 'to be gracious'. It is the language of an appeal to mercy, not of a legal claim.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH Adonai, strength of my salvation, you have covered my head on the day of weaponry.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD God, my strong rescue, you have covered my head on the day the weapons came out.
verses.directors_commentary: The double title 'YHWH Adonai' is a formal, almost heraldic address. The first word is written with the vowels of Elohim (yehovih), the Masoretes' signal that the reader should not pronounce the divine name, so the reading is 'Elohim Adonai': the Targum has 'Elohim YY' and Meiri paraphrases 'you are the God, YHWH'. The KJV's 'O God the Lord' renders that reading rather than reversing the order. 'Strength of my salvation' is a compact phrase: the strength that is my rescue, or the one whose strength brings rescue. 'You have covered my head' (sakkota) uses the verb for roofing a booth or screening a thing with a canopy (sukkah is the same root). The head is covered like a helmet, and Ibn Ezra and Radak read it so: 'a helmet of salvation' (compare Isa 59:17). 'Day of weaponry' (yom nashek) is literal: the Hebrew has 'nashek', 'arms' as a collective, not the KJV's 'battle', which is a gloss. The verb is perfect: it speaks of past rescue, a memory that anchors the present request. Radak adds that a perfect verb can stand for the future, so the line may also be a confident promise.

philological_notes.note: The divine name written with the vowels of Elohim, because it stands beside Adonai and a reader must not say the name twice. The reading is 'Elohim Adonai', as the Targum and Meiri show.

'You have covered, screened'; the root of sukkah, a booth, and of the cherubim's covering wings. Used here for a protective canopy over the head, close to the sense of a helmet (Ibn Ezra on this verse).
Collective 'arms, weaponry', the equipment of a fighter. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'implements of arms'. It is the noun, not the verb 'to kiss'.

verses.translation_literal: Do not grant, YHWH, the desires of a wicked man; his plot do not bring forth; they would rise. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not give them what they crave, LORD, these wicked. Do not let their plot come out into the light, or they will lift their heads high. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the prayer moves from rescue to restraint: not only 'save me' but 'do not let them succeed'. 'Desires' (ma'avayei) is the plural of a rare noun for craving, closely tied to the verb 'to long for'. The wicked's desire is a hunger, which is a stronger picture than the KJV's colourless 'desires'. 'His plot' (zemamo) is another hapax, and the old readings split: Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear 'his scheme', but Rashi also cites the rabbis for 'muzzle', the strap that holds a camel's mouth (a zamam), so the line becomes 'do not let loose his muzzle'. The verb 'taphek' means 'to bring out, to cause to go forth': he has hatched a plan, and the prayer is that it never leaves the heart. The KJV 'further not his wicked device' makes it 'promote', which is acceptable but loses the image of something being brought out. The last word of the clause is 'yarumu' ('they rise'), which the KJV makes into a purpose ('lest they exalt themselves') by supplying 'lest'. The Hebrew gives no 'lest': it has the bare consequence, 'they would rise', and Rashi supplies 'because they will be proud'. Note the swing between singular ('wicked man', 'his plot') and plural ('they rise'): Meiri observes that the singular refers to Doeg and the plural to the whole gang.

philological_notes.note: 'His plot, his scheme' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion, comparing Deut 19:19 'as he plotted'). The rabbis in Rashi also hear a 'muzzle' (zamam), so 'do not release his muzzle'.
Hiphil of puq, 'to bring out'. Radak compares 'and he obtained favour from YHWH' (Prov 8:35). Here: 'do not bring his plot out into action'.

verses.translation_literal: The head of those who surround me: the mischief of their lips, may it cover them.
verses.translation_dramatic: As for the heads of those who ring me round: let the trouble their own lips made close over them.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first of the curses, and it is a mirror: the enemies' own words are turned back. 'Head' (rosh) can mean a leader, as the commentators say (Radak and Metzudat David: Doeg; the Targum: Ahithophel), but it can also be the literal heads of those who encircle him. The KJV's 'the head of those that compass me about' keeps the ambiguity, though 'compass' is archaic for 'surround' and the Hebrew (mesibbai) means 'those who sit around me' or 'those who encircle me', the ring of the siege. 'Mischief' (amal) is more exact as 'toil, trouble, wearing labour': the work their lips have done. The cover is the point. The man who put venom under his lips will find the venom, or the harm he hatched, pulled over his own head, like a cloak (Meiri cites 'he clothed himself with cursing like his garment', Ps 109:18). The verse also echoes verse 8: there YHWH covered the speaker's head (sakak), and here the enemies' heads are covered with their own evil (kasah). The two verbs are different, so this is a thematic mirror rather than a repeated root.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who surround me', from the root 'to go round'. Meiri and Malbim take it as a ring of men closing in; Malbim cites 'Saul and his men were encircling David' (1 Sam 23:26).
'Toil, trouble, mischief': labour that wears people out and that harms. Meiri glosses it 'falsehood and deceit'.

verses.translation_literal: May they be dropped on them, burning coals; into the fire let one make them fall, into pits, so that they do not rise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let burning coals be tipped down on them. Let them be thrown into the fire, into the pits, where they will not get up again.
verses.directors_commentary: The curses turn to fire. 'Burning coals' (gechalim) falling from above recall the fate of Sodom and the burning fall of the wicked in Ps 11:6, and Ibn Ezra and Radak read them as sent from heaven. The verb yamitu ('may they be dropped') is a passive of a root meaning 'to totter, to shake', so the Qere reads 'may they be made to totter, thrown down', and Meiri's reading 'may they be tilted onto them' is the same idea. The hiphil 'yapilem' ('let one make them fall') has no stated subject; the KJV supplies the passive, 'let them be cast', which turns the unnamed hand into a vague agent. The Hebrew keeps the hand hidden, perhaps God, perhaps the fire itself. 'Pits' (mahamorot) is a hapax of unknown meaning: the commentators offer deep pits (Radak, Metzudat Zion, citing the Talmud), quarrels (Rashi) or nets (Meiri); the BBE's 'deep waters' is a guess and so is the KJV's 'deep'. The closing 'bal yaqumu', 'so that they do not get up', uses bal, the poetic negative, which is stronger than 'lo': an emphatic never. The images are grim, but they are the standard curses of covenant lament, and they are a request that the wicked should meet their own trap. Do not play the speaker as gleeful; he is exhausted.

philological_notes.note: Qere reading: 'may they be made to totter, be thrown down'. Rashi: the coals tilt (muttim) onto them until they collapse. Meiri reads the form as 'ymytu' = 'let them tilt down'.
Occurs only here. Radak and Metzudat Zion: deep pits. Meiri: possibly nets (like makhmorot). Rashi: quarrels, linking it to marim (rebels, Deut 9:24). The sense is disputed.

verses.translation_literal: A man of tongue, let him not be established in the land; a man of violence, evil, let it hunt him to thrusts.
verses.translation_dramatic: A man who lives by his tongue: let him find no firm footing in the land. A man of violence: let evil itself hunt him down, thrust after thrust.
verses.directors_commentary: The last line of the window completes the circle: the 'tongue' of verse 4 returns as 'a man of tongue' (ish lashon), a person defined by what he says, a slanderer or a talker. The KJV's 'evil speaker' is fair, though the YLT's 'talkative man' misses the sting. 'Established' (yikkon) is the verb for being set on a firm base, as a house or a throne; so 'let him not be established in the land' wishes him a footless, rootless life. The second line gives the prayer its irony: the hunter becomes the hunted. The trappers of verse 6 now find that 'evil' (ra') is the hunter, and the 'man of violence' is its prey. The Hebrew can be read as 'evil shall hunt him', as a wish or a prediction (the KJV and ASV pick the prediction, 'shall hunt'). The last word, 'madchefot', is a hapax from the root of 'pushing, hurrying'; the KJV 'to overthrow him' and the BBE 'blow on blow' are guesses, as is mine. The image seems to be a hunter driving the prey onward, thrust after thrust, until it falls. Radak and Meiri say the evil he does drives him from one misfortune to the next.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of kun: 'to be set firm, established'. With bal, 'let him not be established': he should have no stable standing in the land. Radak: he shall not be 'firm and lifted up in the land' but will fall to lowness.
A hapax, from dachaf 'to push, to hasten'. 'To thrusts' is literal. Radak and Metzudat David read it as the man being driven 'from evil to evil'; Ibn Ezra, as the people of his land pushing him.

verses.translation_literal: I know that YHWH will do the cause of the poor one, the justice of the needy ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: I know it. After the slander, after the snares and the whispering, one thing stands in me like a stone: the LORD will take up the case of the poor man. He will speak the verdict for those who have nothing.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn from fear to certainty, and it should be played quietly, not triumphantly. The speaker has just listed slanderers and hidden traps; now he says what he knows. In the ancient Near East the poor had no lawyers and no standing, and the king or the elders were supposed to hear their case at the city gate. The Psalm hands that role to YHWH himself, the judge who does not need to be bribed.

The Hebrew says YHWH will "do" the cause (דִּין) and the justice (מִשְׁפָּט): the verbs of the courtroom are plain, working verbs. The KJV's "maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor" is a fair rendering of the pair, and it keeps the parallelism of din / mishpat and of עָנִי (the bowed-down, the afflicted one) and אֶבְיוֹן (the one who begs and wants). Its two small liberties are "maintain", which stands for the plain verb יַעֲשֶׂה, simply "do", and the "and" it supplies, since the Hebrew sets the two halves side by side without one. The singular poor man and the plural needy men also matter: one person speaks, and he speaks for a whole class.

The opening word is a textual puzzle. It is written "you know" (addressed to God) but read aloud "I know". Radak explains both: the written form says "you know that the thoughts of the wicked are against me", and the reading says "I know that he will do justice". Let the actor hold both: a man who trusts that God sees, and so is sure of what comes next.

philological_notes.note: Read (Qere) "I know"; written (Ketiv) יָדַעְתָּ, "you know". The verb of knowing here is a settled conviction, not a guess.
A legal case, a lawsuit, the pleading of a cause; here the thing the judge takes up and settles. It pairs with מִשְׁפָּט, the verdict or right that results.
The needy, the one who lacks and asks; a stronger word of want than עָנִי, which stresses being bowed down or oppressed.

verses.translation_literal: Surely righteous ones will give thanks to your name; upright ones will sit [with] your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, and only then, the righteous will lift their voices and give thanks to your name. And the upright will sit down, at ease, in your presence, face to face, and no longer afraid.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm ends on a calm, almost domestic picture: people sitting down. After a whole poem of running, hiding and ambush, the final image is of the upright sitting, which is what a person does when they are safe at home or guests at a table. Play it as release, not as a victory shout.

The word אַךְ ("surely" in KJV) is sharper than it looks: it means "only" or "nothing but", so Radak reads it as excluding the wicked, who will not give thanks, and Metzudat David reads it the same way, that the righteous alone will praise. The KJV's "surely" keeps the confidence but loses the contrast.

The verb יָשַׁב is "sit" as well as "dwell", and the phrase אֶת־פָּנֶיךָ is literally "with your face", not "in your presence". Ibn Ezra places it in the house of prayer, and Malbim hears more: to sit before the face of the king is to be a courtier who sees him directly. "Thanks" (יוֹדוּ) comes from a verb that also means to confess or to acknowledge publicly: it is thanksgiving said aloud, in front of others, in the name (שֵׁם) of the one who acted. The Targum fills in the gap and has the upright sit to pray before God.

philological_notes.note: A particle of limitation or emphasis: "only" or "surely". Radak takes it to mean that the righteous, and not the wicked, will give thanks.
From a root meaning to throw or confess; in the causative stem it is public thanks or praise, said aloud to the name of the one thanked.
Literally "with your face", the idiom for being in someone's presence. The preposition is unusual after "dwell"; the KJV smooths it to "in thy presence".
